abstract: A large-scale field experiment (N = 5,324) examining the effectiveness of monetary incentives on vaccination uptake. The study finds that guaranteed incentives of $20 increase vaccination rates by 13 percentage points in the short run and 9 percentage points in the long run, with guaranteed incentives proving more effective than lottery-based, prosocial, or individually-targeted approaches. The research demonstrates substantial positive spillovers to relatives and provides guidance on optimal incentive design for public health interventions.
keyFindings: Guaranteed incentives of $20 increase vaccination uptake by 13 percentage points in the short run and 9 percentage points in the long run.
Guaranteed incentives are more effective than lottery-based, prosocial, or individually-targeted incentives, though all approaches boost vaccinations.
There are no unintended consequences on future vaccination behavior or heterogeneous effects based on vaccination attitudes and incentivized economic preferences.
Administrative data on relatives show substantial positive spillovers from the incentive intervention.
methodology: Large-scale field experiment with N = 5,324 participants using a unique combination of administrative and survey data to overcome typical data limitations in vaccination studies. Study design includes comparison of guaranteed incentives, lottery-based incentives, prosocial incentives, and individually-targeted incentives, with administrative data collection on relatives to measure spillover effects.
